supports: ViperGPT gives a code-generation model (Codex) an API to the available vision and language modules and has it compose them into subroutines by generating Python code that is then executed to answer a visual query; the approach needs no further training and reports state-of-the-art zero-shot results across several complex visual tasks (RefCOCO grounding, GQA, OK-VQA and NExT-QA).
doesNotEstablish: The code generator is a large prompted model (Codex) given a hand-written API specification, not a small fine-tuned model, and the evidence is final-answer accuracy on visual benchmarks, not a separate measure of the correctness of the generated programs.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: SatLM: Satisfiability-Aided Language Models Using Declarative Prompting
metadata: Crossref DOI record and NeurIPS 2023 proceedings page (Main Conference Track), accessed 2026-09-29; title, authors, venue, volume, pages and year checked.
locator: Abstract; Section 3.2 (Solving with a SAT Solver)
supports: SatLM has an LLM write a declarative task specification instead of an imperative program and leaves the reasoning to an off-the-shelf automated theorem prover (the Z3 SMT solver in the implementation), which guarantees the answer is correct with respect to the parsed specification; across 8 datasets it consistently outperforms program-aided LMs in the imperative paradigm, by 23% on a challenging subset of GSM.
doesNotEstablish: The guarantee holds only relative to the parsed specification, so a mis-parsed problem still yields a wrong answer, and the experiments prompt large OpenAI models (mainly code-davinci-002) rather than fine-tuning small models.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: Logic-LM: Empowering Large Language Models with Symbolic Solvers for Faithful Logical Reasoning
metadata: Crossref DOI record, ACL Anthology BibTeX and published PDF, accessed 2026-09-29; title, authors, venue, pages and year checked; Crossref and the Anthology list the fourth author as William Wang, the PDF byline as William Yang Wang, whose initials are used here.
locator: Abstract; Sections 3.1-3.3 (Problem Formulator, Symbolic Reasoner, Self-Refiner)
supports: Logic-LM has an LLM translate a natural-language logical problem into a symbolic formulation, a deterministic symbolic solver then performs the inference, and a self-refinement module feeds the solver's error messages back to the LLM to revise the formulation; on five logical reasoning datasets it improves on the same LLM by 39.2% over standard prompting and 18.4% over chain-of-thought prompting on average.
doesNotEstablish: The formulations come from few-shot prompting of gpt-3.5-turbo, text-davinci-003 and GPT-4 rather than fine-tuned small models, the tasks are logical reasoning benchmarks rather than program generation, and self-refinement is triggered only by solver execution errors, so formulations that run but are wrong are not revised.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: PICARD: Parsing Incrementally for Constrained Auto-Regressive Decoding from Language Models
metadata: Crossref DOI record and ACL Anthology BibTeX, accessed 2026-09-29; title, authors, venue, pages and year checked.
supports: Language models fine-tuned to a formal language such as SQL often generate invalid code; PICARD constrains the auto-regressive decoder through incremental parsing, rejecting inadmissible tokens at each decoding step so that valid output sequences are found, and on the Spider and CoSQL text-to-SQL tasks it turns fine-tuned T5 models with passable performance into state-of-the-art solutions.
doesNotEstablish: The checks cover SQL lexing, parsing and schema-dependent guards (for example valid table and column names), so they exclude invalid SQL but not valid queries that answer the wrong question, and the evidence is for fine-tuned T5 models on two text-to-SQL benchmarks.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: Synchromesh: Reliable Code Generation from Pre-trained Language Models
metadata: ICLR 2022 conference data and poster page (iclr.cc virtual poster 6709, decision Accept (Poster), linking OpenReview forum KmtVD97J43e) and arXiv:2201.11227v1, accessed 2026-09-29; title, authors, venue and year checked; no DOI and no page range (ICLR 2022 is not on proceedings.iclr.cc, and direct OpenReview access returned a browser challenge). The ICLR listing names the second author Alex Polozov; the paper byline on arXiv gives Oleksandr Polozov, whose initial is used here.
supports: Synchromesh retrieves few-shot examples with Target Similarity Tuning, which learns to select examples whose target programs are similar, and then samples programs with Constrained Semantic Decoding, which uses constraints on partial outputs to restrict a pre-trained model to valid programs of the target language without re-training or fine-tuning; with GPT-3 and Codex on SQL, Vega-Lite and SMCalFlow it enforces syntax, scoping and typing rules and gives complementary gains in accuracy and in preventing parsing, type and run-time errors.
doesNotEstablish: Constrained decoding rules out invalid programs but does not make a valid program semantically correct, and the evidence is for few-shot prompting of large models (GPT-3 and Codex), not for fine-tuned small models.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: Constrained Language Models Yield Few-Shot Semantic Parsers
metadata: Crossref DOI record, ACL Anthology BibTeX and published PDF, accessed 2026-09-29; title, authors, venue, pages and year checked; Crossref and the Anthology list the second author as Christopher Lin, the PDF byline as Christopher H. Lin, whose initials are used here.
locator: Abstract; Section 1 (Introduction) and Figure 1; Section 3 (Approach, Constrained Decoding)
supports: A pretrained language model (GPT-3 primed with a few examples, or a fine-tuned BART or GPT-2) paraphrases the input into a controlled, English-like sublanguage of canonical utterances; a grammar constrains decoding to canonical utterances, which map mechanically to the target meaning representation, and with little data this yields few-shot semantic parsers that greatly exceed baselines trained on the same limited data (Overnight, Break and SMCalFlow).
doesNotEstablish: The approach relies on a developer-written synchronous grammar that pairs canonical utterances with meaning representations, the authors do not expect it to match parsers trained on large task-specific data, and the evidence is for semantic parsing datasets rather than general program generation.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: Grammar-Constrained Decoding for Structured NLP Tasks without Finetuning
metadata: Crossref DOI record and ACL Anthology BibTeX, accessed 2026-09-29; title, authors, venue, pages and year checked.
supports: Formal grammars can describe the output space of a wide range of structured NLP tasks, and grammar-constrained decoding guarantees that a language model's output follows the required structure; input-dependent grammars let the grammar depend on the input, and with few-shot-prompted LLaMA and Vicuna models and no fine-tuning, grammar-constrained models substantially outperform unconstrained ones, or even beat task-specific fine-tuned models, on closed information extraction, entity disambiguation and constituency parsing.
doesNotEstablish: The guarantee is structural (the output conforms to the grammar), not semantic correctness, and the evidence covers three NLP tasks with LLaMA (7B to 33B) and Vicuna (7B and 13B), not code or program generation.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: Advances in dataflow programming languages
metadata: Crossref DOI record, accessed 2026-09-29; title, authors, venue, volume, issue, pages and year checked. The Crossref abstract describes the survey's scope but does not state the definition; the published full text (ACM Computing Surveys 36(1), pp. 1-34) was read from a course-hosted copy (cs.tufts.edu/comp/150CMP) because the ACM Digital Library returned a browser challenge.
locator: Section 1 (Introduction); Section 2.1 (The Pure Dataflow Model); Section 3.1.1 (What Constitutes a Dataflow Programming Language?)
supports: In the dataflow execution model a program is a directed graph whose nodes are operations and whose arcs carry the data dependencies between them; a node becomes fireable when data are present on its input arcs, so instructions are scheduled for execution as soon as their operands become available, in contrast to the von Neumann model where an instruction runs only when the program counter reaches it; under the single-assignment rule the order of statements in a dataflow language does not matter, except when a loop is defined.
doesNotEstablish: The survey reviews dataflow languages and architectures up to 2004 and does not address generating dataflow programs with neural models or using them as model targets.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: Top-Down Synthesis for Library Learning
metadata: Crossref DOI record, accessed 2026-09-29; title, authors, venue, volume, issue, pages and year checked.
supports: Corpus-guided top-down synthesis builds library functions (abstractions) that capture functionality shared across a corpus of DSL programs directly from the DSL primitives, pruning the search with syntactic pattern matching; the Stitch implementation is 3-4 orders of magnitude faster and uses 2 orders of magnitude less memory than DreamCoder's deductive library learning while keeping comparable or better library quality (compressivity), and it scales to corpora of hundreds of complex programs.
doesNotEstablish: Library quality is measured as compression of a given program corpus, and the abstract reports no test of whether the learned abstractions help a neural model generate programs.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: LILO: Learning Interpretable Libraries by Compressing and Documenting Code
metadata: ICLR 2024 proceedings record and BibTeX (proceedings.iclr.cc, pages 30399-30446), ICLR 2024 conference data (poster 18550, decision Accept (poster), OpenReview forum TqYbAWKMIe) and arXiv:2310.19791v4 metadata (comment: ICLR 2024 camera-ready), accessed 2026-09-29; title, authors, venue, pages and year checked; no DOI; direct OpenReview access returned a browser challenge.
supports: LILO iteratively synthesizes, compresses and documents code to build libraries for a problem domain: it combines LLM-guided program synthesis with automated refactoring by Stitch, a symbolic compression system that identifies optimal lambda abstractions across a code corpus, and an auto-documentation procedure (AutoDoc) that infers natural-language names and docstrings from usage examples, which also helps the synthesizer use the learned abstractions; on string editing, scene reasoning and graphics composition it solves more complex tasks and learns richer libraries than DreamCoder and other neural and symbolic methods.
doesNotEstablish: The synthesizer is a large prompted model (Codex, with gpt-3.5-turbo and gpt-4 for AutoDoc) rather than a small fine-tuned model, and the evaluation covers three inductive program-synthesis domains (REGEX, CLEVR and LOGO), not the compilation of natural-language problems.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: How accurate is scientific software?
metadata: Crossref DOI record 10.1109/32.328993 and OpenAlex record with abstract, accessed 2026-09-29; title, authors, journal, volume 20, issue 10, pages 785-797 and year checked.
supports: In an N-version experiment, nine independently developed commercial seismic data-processing packages given the same input data and parameters disagreed numerically, the disagreement growing by about 1% in average absolute difference per 4,000 lines of code and being non-random.
doesNotEstablish: Concerns numerical code in one domain in 1994; does not address machine-learning pipelines or errors of interpretation.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?

doesNotEstablish: Does not study research pipelines operated by coding agents over days, or the detection of errors after the fact.

title: Ironies of automation
metadata: Crossref DOI record 10.1016/0005-1098(83)90046-8, accessed 2026-09-29; title, author, journal, volume 19, issue 6, pages 775-779 and year checked against the article's first page.
locator: Abstract and Section 1 (p. 775); the discussion of monitoring (p. 776); read from an open copy of the article
supports: Automation may expand rather than eliminate problems with the human operator: the designer who tries to eliminate the operator still leaves the operator the tasks that could not be automated, including monitoring that the automatic system is operating correctly, and even a highly motivated person cannot maintain effective visual attention on a source on which very little happens for more than about half an hour.
doesNotEstablish: Concerns process control and flight decks, not software pipelines or coding agents.
status: Primary-source support checked for the limited proposition recorded here.
